summary: In Greek mythology, Adrastus son of Merops of Percote co-leads the Trojan allies from Adrasteia and neighboring towns with his brother Amphius (atlas Araphius). Ignoring their father's prophetic warning, both fall to Diomedes. He is not Adrastus of Argos, nor the Trojan whom Agamemnon slays after Menelaus' ransom plea, nor Patroclus' victim.
etymology: Ancient Greek Ἄδραστος / Ἄδρηστος, perhaps "the inescapable"; here the name may also echo the district Adrasteia.

sections.heading: Son of Merops at Troy
paragraphs: Homer and Apollodorus place Adrastus and Amphius, sons of the seer Merops of Percote, at the head of allies from Adrasteia, Apaesus, Pityeia, and Tereia. Merops foresaw their deaths and forbade the war; the brothers went nonetheless.

Diomedes kills both in Iliad 11. Some modern commentators identify this Adrastus with the ransom-victim of Iliad 6; others (and this atlas) keep adrastus-trojan-ransom as a separate node, noting the poem would otherwise contradict itself on who kills him.

sections.heading: Homonym care
paragraphs: The atlas id adrastus-meropsid is Merops' Percotean son alone. Distinct from adrastus (Argive leader of the Seven), adrastus-trojan-ransom (Menelaus' captive), adrastus-trojan (Patroclus' victim), and the Lydian Adrastus son of Gordias in Herodotus.
